teaching.en: When a foreign colleague's words seem unfriendly, it is wiser to give the benefit of the doubt and ask them to clarify.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato y elige qué aclara Ana sobre su costumbre.

choices.text: She says maybe when she really means no.
She never uses the word maybe with colleagues.
Saying maybe is her polite habit, not a refusal.

feedback.es: Ana explica que maybe es una forma cortés de mantener la conversación, no un rechazo ni una promesa.

origin.audio: Ana, who comes from Ecuador, told her new colleague Luna that in her country it is a custom to say maybe when you want to be polite. She explained that for her, maybe was never a promise or a refusal, only a way of keeping the conversation warm. Luna had taken it as a no, and she was surprised. She thanked Ana for clarifying it, and said that in her own country maybe often does mean no.

prompt.es: Escribe el mensaje de reparación de Mia a Tom (unas 170 palabras).

answer.text: Dear Tom, I think there was a misunderstanding at the dinner on Friday, and I would like to clear the air. I did not intend to offend you, and I am very sorry that my insistence on paying may have come across as rude. In my country it is a custom for the person who invites to pay for everybody, and refusing your offer was my way of showing respect, not of ignoring you. I can see now that it may have given the wrong impression, since in Scotland friends usually share the bill. I apologise for not explaining this at the time, and I hope you will give me the benefit of the doubt. Let me clarify something else: I enjoyed the evening very much, and I appreciate your honesty when you told me how you felt. Perhaps we could meet halfway next time: I will choose the restaurant, and you will pay for the dessert. Would you like to have lunch on Saturday? I promise to ask before I reach for the bill. Kind regards, Mia
accepted: Dear Tom, I think there was a misunderstanding at the dinner on Friday, and I would like to clear the air. I did not intend to offend you, and I am very sorry that my insistence on paying may have come across as rude. In my country it is a custom for the person who invites to pay for everybody, and refusing your offer was my way of showing respect, not of ignoring you. I can see now that it may have given the wrong impression, since in Scotland friends usually share the bill. I apologise for not explaining this at the time, and I hope you will give me the benefit of the doubt. Let me clarify something else: I enjoyed the evening very much, and I appreciate your honesty when you told me how you felt. Perhaps we could meet halfway next time: I will choose the restaurant, and you will pay for the dessert. Would you like to have lunch on Saturday? I promise to ask before I reach for the bill. Kind regards, Mia

Hello Tom, I am sorry about the confusion at the dinner. I think we had a misunderstanding, and I never meant to hurt you. Where I come from, the person who invites usually pays for everybody, so when I refused your offer I wanted to show respect, but I see that it may have given the wrong impression and come across as rude to you. I apologise for not explaining that at the moment. Let me clarify: I had a lovely evening, and I want to keep our friendship. I appreciate that you told me how you felt, and I hope you can give me the benefit of the doubt. Perhaps we could go out again on Saturday, and this time we could split the bill so that nobody feels uncomfortable. Would you like that? Thank you for listening.

feedback.es: Un buen mensaje nombra el malentendido, aclara la intención, se disculpa, explica la costumbre, agradece la sinceridad y propone seguir adelante.

origin.text: Mia, de Ecuador, insistió en pagar toda la cena; Tom, de Escocia, creyó que ella ignoraba su oferta de dividir la cuenta y se fue temprano, ofendido. Escribe el mensaje de Mia: nombra el malentendido, aclara tu intención, discúlpate, explica la costumbre, da las gracias por su sinceridad y propón un plan nuevo.

prompt.es: ¿Qué concluyen Tom y Mia sobre el malentendido?

choices.text: That Tom should have asked more questions about the invitation before answering.
That the same word carries a different value in each country, and nobody was at fault.
That Mia should stop using the word maybe with people from Scotland.
That the misunderstanding was caused by Tom's lack of good manners.

feedback.es: Los dos reconocen que usaron la misma palabra con valores distintos y que ninguno fue grosero: el malentendido es cultural, no una falta de nadie.

origin.text: Tom explained that in Scotland maybe often means no, so he had taken Mia's answer as a refusal. Mia explained that in Ecuador maybe can be a polite way of saying that you are not sure, and that she had never meant to reject him. Both agreed that neither of them had been rude; they had simply been using the same word in different ways.

origin.audio: Leo wrote back to Mia the same evening. He said that he was sorry that his answer had sounded unfriendly, that he had not meant it that way, and that he would like to start again. He added that he would gladly give her the benefit of the doubt, if she would do the same for him.
